subject: psych
title: Pluralistic ignorance: when everyone privately disagrees with a norm that no one supports
dek: Sometimes most people in a group privately reject a norm, yet each person believes they are the only one who feels that way, so the norm survives. This lesson explains the concept first, then follows the Princeton drinking study and a field experiment on women's work in Saudi Arabia.
era: Allport 1924; term coined by Katz and Allport 1931; O'Gorman 1975; Miller and McFarland 1987; Prentice and Miller 1993; Bursztyn and colleagues 2020
honesty: This lesson is text only. Study details are summarized from the published papers as described in secondary sources, and specific percentages are left out where I could not confirm them.

timeline.label: Andersen's The Emperor's New Clothes
timeline.detail: Hans Christian Andersen's tale, in which a crowd praises invisible clothes until a child says the emperor has nothing on, became the standard literary illustration of the idea.

timeline.label: Floyd Allport describes the problem
timeline.detail: Allport noted that people often conform to norms they do not personally agree with, and suggested they act on their convictions only when they believe others share them.

timeline.label: The term appears
timeline.detail: Daniel Katz and Floyd Allport used the phrase 'pluralistic ignorance' in Students' Attitudes, their report on a study of Syracuse University students.

timeline.label: O'Gorman on segregation
timeline.detail: Hubert O'Gorman showed that white Americans overestimated how much other white Americans supported racial segregation.

timeline.label: Miller and McFarland
timeline.detail: Dale Miller and Cathy McFarland showed experimentally how people read their own hesitation as fear but read the same hesitation in others as real confidence.

timeline.label: Prentice and Miller's drinking study
timeline.detail: Deborah Prentice and Dale Miller found that Princeton students were less comfortable with campus drinking than they believed the average student was.

timeline.label: Saudi Arabia field experiment
timeline.detail: Leonardo Bursztyn, Alessandra González and David Yanagizawa-Drott showed that correcting men's beliefs about other men's views changed their behavior.

blocks.text: Pluralistic ignorance is a situation in which most members of a group privately reject a belief or a norm, but each of them wrongly assumes that most of the others accept it. Because everyone thinks they are in the minority, few people say what they really think, and many go along with the norm in public. The result is a norm that is followed by many people and supported by few.

The important point is that the mistake is about other people's minds, not about one's own. A student who privately thinks heavy drinking is unpleasant is not confused about their own view. They are confused about how common that view is. Psychologists sometimes describe this as an error in 'second-order beliefs', which means beliefs about what other people believe.

The error tends to keep itself going. If I hide my doubts, other people see me going along and conclude that I support the norm. They hide their doubts too, and I see them going along. Every person's public behavior becomes false evidence for everyone else. This is why a norm can last long after private opinion has moved on, a delay that researchers call the conservative lag.

The concept is related to, but different from, several other ideas. The false consensus effect is the opposite error, in which people assume that others agree with them more than they really do. The spiral of silence, a theory from the German researcher Elisabeth Noelle-Neumann, describes how people who think their opinion is unpopular stay quiet, which makes it look even less popular. Groupthink and the bystander effect are often described as consequences of pluralistic ignorance: in a meeting, each doubter sees the others nodding, and in an emergency, each bystander sees the others standing still and concludes that nothing is wrong.

sections.title: From Allport's students to the segregation surveys

blocks.text: The American psychologist Floyd Allport first wrote about the problem in 1924. He was interested in why people follow social rules that they do not personally endorse. His answer was that people usually act on their own convictions only when they believe those convictions are shared. In 1931 Allport and his student Daniel Katz used the term pluralistic ignorance in Students' Attitudes, a report on a large survey of Syracuse University students.

Much of the later work came from sociologists and public opinion researchers rather than laboratory psychologists, because the phenomenon is easiest to see in surveys that ask people both what they think and what they believe others think. A well-known example is Hubert O'Gorman's 1975 paper in Public Opinion Quarterly. Using survey data from the late 1960s, he showed that white Americans substantially overestimated how many other white Americans supported racial segregation. Private attitudes had shifted faster than people realized, and the mistaken picture of majority opinion helped keep segregationist norms in place.

In 1987 Dale Miller and Cathy McFarland gave the idea an experimental basis. In their studies, people who held back because they were afraid of looking foolish assumed that others who held back had a different, more confident reason. A familiar version is the classroom: a student who does not understand the lecture stays silent out of embarrassment, sees that nobody else asks a question, and concludes that everyone else understood.

sections.title: Drinking at Princeton: Prentice and Miller, 1993

blocks.text: The best-known study of pluralistic ignorance was published in 1993 by Deborah Prentice and Dale Miller in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, under the title 'Pluralistic ignorance and alcohol use on campus: Some consequences of misperceiving the social norm.' Drinking was a central part of social life at Princeton, and Prentice and Miller suspected that many students were less enthusiastic about it than they appeared.

They asked students how comfortable they personally were with drinking habits on campus, and how comfortable they thought the average Princeton student was. On average, students rated their own comfort lower than the comfort they attributed to the typical student. In other words, most students thought they were more uneasy than their peers, when in fact their peers felt much the same way.

The researchers then followed students over a semester. Among men, private attitudes gradually moved toward the norm they believed existed. The men came to feel more comfortable with drinking, which is what cognitive dissonance theory would predict when people repeatedly behave in a way that does not match their attitudes. Women showed no similar shift. Prentice and Miller also found that students who felt they deviated from the drinking norm reported more alienation from campus life, even though the deviance was mostly imagined.

The study had practical influence. It supported the 'social norms' approach to campus alcohol programs, in which universities publish survey results showing students how much their peers actually drink and how they actually feel about it. The idea is that correcting the false picture of the norm removes some of the pressure to follow it. The results of these campaigns have been mixed, and researchers still debate how well they work.

sections.title: Women working outside the home in Saudi Arabia

blocks.text: A 2020 study in the American Economic Review by Leonardo Bursztyn, Alessandra González and David Yanagizawa-Drott tested whether correcting pluralistic ignorance changes real decisions. They surveyed young married men in Saudi Arabia. The large majority privately supported women working outside the home, but the men greatly underestimated how many other men like them shared that view.

The researchers then told some of the men the true level of support among their peers. Men who received this information were more likely to help their wives obtain jobs, for example by signing them up for a job-matching service. The study is valuable because it moves beyond attitudes on a questionnaire and shows that a mistaken belief about other people's views can hold back behavior, and that correcting it can release that behavior.

Pluralistic ignorance helps explain why social change can seem to happen suddenly. When private opinion has shifted but public behavior has not, a single visible act, a published survey, or a person who speaks first can reveal that the supposed majority was never there. Researchers have used the idea to discuss the collapse of support for unpopular regimes, changing attitudes toward race and gender, and present-day issues such as climate change, where surveys suggest that many people who want stronger action believe they are in the minority.

The concept also has limits. It describes a gap between private views and perceived norms, but it does not by itself explain how that gap formed. Measuring private attitudes is difficult, because people may not report them honestly even in anonymous surveys. And not every unpopular-looking norm is held in place by misperception; sometimes people stay quiet because speaking up carries real penalties, not just imagined ones.

Think of a habit or rule in a group you belong to, such as a workplace, a class, or a family. Do you suspect that more people privately dislike it than anyone admits? What would it take for someone to find out?

fun_fact.title: The idea has a century-long research history
fun_fact.text: Dale Miller, who co-wrote both the 1987 classroom study and the 1993 Princeton drinking study, published a review in 2023 titled 'A century of pluralistic ignorance', counting from Floyd Allport's first discussion of the problem in 1924.
